channel.title: Eat Safe Japan — gluten-free
channel.description: Gluten-free, vegan, halal and allergy-friendly eating in Japan — explained by locals.

item.title: Is Miso Gluten-Free? What Coeliacs Need to Know
item.description: Miso can be made from rice, barley or soybeans alone — and only one of those is a problem for coeliacs. Here's how to read Japanese miso labels, spot barley miso (mugi miso), and ask restaurant staff the right questions before your bowl of miso soup arrives.

item.title: Gluten-Free Osaka: What Coeliacs Need to Know
item.description: Osaka is Japan's street food capital, but its two most famous dishes—okonomiyaki and takoyaki—are built on wheat batter and shared grills. Here's what's actually in them, why cross-contact is hard to avoid, and which Osaka dishes are genuinely easier for coeliacs to navigate, plus the Japanese phrases to use when ordering.

item.title: Is Sushi Gluten-Free in Japan? What Coeliacs Must Know
item.description: Plain fish on rice looks like the safest meal in Japan, but soy sauce, imitation crab, tamago and eel sauce can all contain wheat. This guide walks through what's actually in a sushi set, how cross-contact happens at the counter and on conveyor belts, and exactly what to say to staff before you order.

item.title: Gluten-Free Konbini Shopping: What to Check in Japan
item.description: Konbini food looks simple, but hidden wheat shows up in soy sauce seasoning, dressings and even rice snacks. This guide shows coeliac and gluten-free travellers exactly how to read Japanese convenience store labels — onigiri, salads, bento and snacks — so you can shop with confidence, not guesswork.

item.title: Gluten-Free Kyoto: Kaiseki & Temple Food Guide
item.description: Planning a coeliac-friendly trip to Kyoto? Here's what you need to know about hidden wheat in kaiseki ryori, shojin ryori temple cuisine, soy sauce and wheat gluten (fu) before you book a single meal — plus the exact Japanese phrases to use at the table.

item.title: Is Ramen Gluten-Free? What Coeliacs Need to Know
item.description: Ramen looks like a bowl of noodles and broth, but wheat hides in more places than just the noodles — the tare, the soup base, the toppings, even the gyoza on the side menu. This guide breaks down exactly where gluten comes from in a typical bowl of ramen in Japan, what to ask staff, and where to look for genuinely gluten-free alternatives.

item.title: The Real Way to Eat Gluten-Free in Tokyo
item.description: Gluten-free in Tokyo isn't impossible, but it does take strategy. Learn which restaurant types are worth your time, where wheat hides in Japanese cooking (soy sauce, miso, breading), and the exact Japanese phrases to use so kitchen staff understand your request. A practical, safety-first guide for coeliacs and anyone avoiding gluten.

item.title: Is Soy Sauce Gluten-Free in Japan? (Usually Not)
item.description: Travelling to Japan with coeliac disease or a gluten intolerance? Most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat and it hides in sauces, broths and snacks. Learn how to read wheat-free labels, what tamari really means, and the Japanese phrases to ask staff for safer options.
